text: There was once upon a time a poor widow who had an only son named Jack, and a cow named Milky-white. And all they had to live on was the milk the cow gave every morning which they carried to the market and sold. But one morning Milky-white gave no milk and they didn't know what to do. “What shall we do, what shall we do?” said the widow, wringing her hands. “Cheer up, mother, I'll go and get work somewhere,” said Jack. “We've tried that before, and nobody would take you,” said his mother; “we must sell Milky-white and with the money do something, start shop, or something.” “All right, mother,” says Jack; “it's market-day today, and I'll soon sell Milky-white, and then we'll see what we can do.” So he took the cow's halter in his hand, and off he starts. He hadn't gone far when he met a funny-looking old man who said to him: “Good morning, Jack.” “Good morning to you,” said Jack, and wondered how he knew his name. “Well, Jack, and where are you off to?” said the man. “I'm going to market to sell our cow here.” “Oh, you look the proper sort of chap to sell cows,” said the man; “I wonder if you know how many beans make five.” “Two in each hand and one in your mouth,” says Jack, as sharp as a needle. “Right you are,” said the man, “and here they are the very beans themselves,” he went on pulling out of his pocket a number of strange-looking beans. “As you are so sharp,” says he, “I don't mind doing a swop with you--your cow for these beans.” “Walker!” says Jack; “wouldn't you like it?” “Ah! you don't know what these beans are,” said the man; “if you plant them over-night, by morning they grow right up to the sky.” “Really?” says Jack; “you don't say so.” “Yes, that is so, and if it doesn't turn out to be true you can have your cow back.” “Right,” says Jack, and hands him over Milky-white's halter and pockets the beans. Back goes Jack home, and as he hadn't gone very far it wasn't dusk by the time he got to his door. “What back, Jack?” said his mother; “I see you haven't got Milky-white, so you've sold her. How much did you get for her?” “You'll never guess, mother,” says Jack. “No, you don't say so. Good boy! Five pounds, ten, fifteen, no, it can't be twenty.” “I told you you couldn't guess, what do you say to these beans; they're magical, plant them over-night and----” “What!” says Jack's mother, “have you been such a fool, such a dolt, such an idiot, as to give away my Milky-white, the best milker in the parish, and prime beef to boot, for a set of paltry beans. Take that! Take that! Take that! And as for your precious beans here they go out of the window. And now off with you to bed. Not a sup shall you drink, and not a bit shall you swallow this very night.” So Jack went upstairs to his little room in the attic, and sad and sorry he was, to be sure, as much for his mother's sake, as for the loss of his supper. At last he dropped off to sleep. When he woke up, the room looked so funny. The sun was shining into part of it, and yet all the rest was quite dark and shady. So Jack jumped up and dressed himself and went to the window. And what do you think he saw? why, the beans his mother had thrown out of the window into the garden, had sprung up into a big beanstalk which went up and up and up till it reached the sky. So the man spoke truth after all. The beanstalk grew up quite close past Jack's window, so all he had to do was to open it and give a jump on to the beanstalk which was made like a big plaited ladder. So Jack climbed and he climbed and he climbed and he climbed and he climbed and he climbed and he climbed till at last he reached the sky. And when he got there he found a long broad road going as straight as a dart. So he walked along and he walked along and he walked along till he came to a great big tall house, and on the doorstep there was a great big tall woman. “Good morning, mum,” says Jack, quite polite-like. “Could you be so kind as to give me some breakfast.” For he hadn't had anything to eat, you know, the night before and was as hungry as a hunter. “It's breakfast you want, is it?” says the great big tall woman, “it's breakfast you'll be if you don't move off from here. My man is an ogre and there's nothing he likes better than boys broiled on toast. You'd better be moving on or he'll soon be coming.” “Oh! please mum, do give me something to eat, mum. I've had nothing to eat since yesterday morning, really and truly, mum,” says Jack. “I may as well be broiled, as die of hunger.” Well, the ogre's wife wasn't such a bad sort, after all. So she took Jack into the kitchen, and gave him a junk of bread and cheese and a jug of milk. But Jack hadn't half finished these when thump! thump! thump! the whole house began to tremble with the noise of someone coming. “Goodness gracious me! It's my old man,” said the ogre's wife, “what on earth shall I do? Here, come quick and jump in here.” And she bundled Jack into the oven just as the ogre came in. He was a big one, to be sure. At his belt he had three calves strung up by the heels, and he unhooked them and threw them down on the table and said: “Here, wife, broil me a couple of these for breakfast. Ah what's this I smell? Fee-fi-fo-fum, I smell the blood of an Englishman, Be he alive, or be he dead I'll have his bones to grind my bread.” “Nonsense, dear,” said his wife, “you're dreaming. Or perhaps you smell the scraps of that little boy you liked so much for yesterday's dinner. Here, go you and have a wash and tidy up, and by the time you come back your breakfast'll be ready for you.” So the ogre went off, and Jack was just going to jump out of the oven and run off when the woman told him not. “Wait till he's asleep,” says she; “he always has a snooze after breakfast.” Well, the ogre had his breakfast, and after that he goes to a big chest and takes out of it a couple of bags of gold and sits down counting them till at last his head began to nod and he began to snore till the whole house shook again. Then Jack crept out on tiptoe from his oven, and as he was passing the ogre he took one of the bags of gold under his arm, and off he pelters till he came to the beanstalk, and then he threw down the bag of gold which of course fell in to his mother's garden, and then he climbed down and climbed down till at last he got home and told his mother and showed her the gold and said: “Well, mother, wasn't I right about the beans. They are really magical, you see.” So they lived on the bag of gold for some time, but at last they came to the end of that so Jack made up his mind to try his luck once more up at the top of the beanstalk. So one fine morning he got up early, and got on to the beanstalk, and he climbed and he climbed and he climbed and he climbed and he climbed and he climbed till at last he got on the road again and came to the great big tall house he had been to before. There, sure enough, was the great big tall woman a-standing on the door-step. “Good morning, mum,” says Jack, as bold as brass, “could you be so good as to give me something to eat?” “Go away, my boy,” said the big, tall woman, “or else my man will eat you up for breakfast. But aren't you the youngster who came here once before? Do you know, that very day, my man missed one of his bags of gold.” “That's strange, mum,” says Jack, “I dare say I could tell you something about that but I'm so hungry I can't speak till I've had something to eat.” Well the big tall woman was that curious that she took him in and gave him something to eat. But he had scarcely begun munching it as slowly as he could when thump! thump! thump! they heard the giant's footstep, and his wife hid Jack away in the oven. All happened as it did before. In came the ogre as he did before, said: “Fee-fi-fo-fum,” and had his breakfast off three broiled oxen. Then he said: “Wife, bring me the hen that lays the golden eggs.” So she brought it, and the ogre said: “Lay,” and it laid an egg all of gold. And then the ogre began to nod his head, and to snore till the house shook. Then Jack crept out of the oven on tiptoe and caught hold of the golden hen, and was off before you could say “Jack Robinson.” But this time the hen gave a cackle which woke the ogre, and just as Jack got out of the house he heard him calling: “Wife, wife, what have you done with my golden hen?” And the wife said: “Why, my dear?” But that was all Jack heard, for he rushed off to the beanstalk and climbed down like a house on fire. And when he got home he showed his mother the wonderful hen and said “Lay,” to it; and it laid a golden egg every time he said “Lay.” Well, Jack was not content, and it wasn't very long before he determined to have another try at his luck up there at the top of the beanstalk. So one fine morning, he got up early, and went on to the beanstalk, and he climbed and he climbed and he climbed and he climbed till he got to the top. But this time he knew better than to go straight to the ogre's house. And when he got near it he waited behind a bush till he saw the ogre's wife come out with a pail to get some water, and then he crept into the house and got into the copper. He hadn't been there long when he heard thump! thump! thump! as before, and in come the ogre and his wife. “Fee-fi-fo-fum, I smell the blood of an Englishman,” cried out the ogre; “I smell him, wife, I smell him.” “Do you, my dearie?” says the ogre's wife. “Then if it's that little rogue that stole your gold and the hen that laid the golden eggs he's sure to have got into the oven.” And they both rushed to the oven. But Jack wasn't there, luckily, and the ogre's wife said: “There you are again with your fee-fi-fo-fum. Why of course it's the laddie you caught last night that I've broiled for your breakfast. How forgetful I am, and how careless you are not to tell the difference between a live un and a dead un.” So the ogre sat down to the breakfast and ate it, but every now and then he would mutter: “Well, I could have sworn----” and he'd get up and search the larder and the cupboards, and everything, only luckily he didn't think of the copper. After breakfast was over, the ogre called out: “Wife, wife, bring me my golden harp.” So she brought it and put it on the table before him. Then he said: “Sing!” and the golden harp sang most beautifully. And it went on singing till the ogre fell asleep, and commenced to snore like thunder. Then Jack lifted up the copper-lid very quietly and got down like a mouse and crept on hands and knees till he got to the table when he got up and caught hold of the golden harp and dashed with it towards the door. But the harp called out quite loud: “Master! Master!” and the ogre woke up just in time to see Jack running off with his harp. Jack ran as fast as he could, and the ogre came rushing after, and would soon have caught him only Jack had a start and dodged him a bit and knew where he was going. When he got to the beanstalk the ogre was not more than twenty yards away when suddenly he saw Jack disappear like, and when he got up to the end of the road he saw Jack underneath climbing down for dear life. Well, the ogre didn't like trusting himself to such a ladder, and he stood and waited, so Jack got another start. But just then the harp cried out: “Master! master!” and the ogre swung himself down on to the beanstalk which shook with his weight. Down climbs Jack, and after him climbed the ogre. By this time Jack had climbed down and climbed down and climbed down till he was very nearly home. So he called out: “Mother! mother! bring me an axe, bring me an axe.” And his mother came rushing out with the axe in her hand, but when she came to the beanstalk she stood stock still with fright for there she saw the ogre just coming down below the clouds. But Jack jumped down and got hold of the axe and gave a chop at the beanstalk which cut it half in two. The ogre felt the beanstalk shake and quiver so he stopped to see what was the matter. Then Jack gave another chop with the axe, and the beanstalk was cut in two and began to topple over. Then the ogre fell down and broke his crown, and the beanstalk came toppling after. Then Jack showed his mother his golden harp, and what with showing that and selling the golden eggs, Jack and his mother became very rich, and he married a great princess, and they lived happy ever after.

sentences.korean: "오, 너는 소를 팔기에 적합한 친구로 보이는구나," 노인이 말했습니다. "너는 콩 다섯 개가 몇 개인지 아는지 궁금하구나."

sentences.physical_context: Jack confidently answers the old man's riddle.
sentences.korean: "양손에 두 개씩, 입에 하나," 잭이 바늘처럼 날카롭게 대답했습니다.

sentences.physical_context: The old man reveals the beans from his pocket.
sentences.korean: "맞아," 노인이 말했습니다. "그리고 여기 바로 그 콩들이 있단다," 그는 주머니에서 이상하게 생긴 콩들을 꺼내며 말했습니다.

sentences.physical_context: The old man offers to trade the beans for the cow.
sentences.korean: "너는 정말 똑똑하구나," 그가 말했습니다. "나는 너와 교환해도 상관없어 - 너의 소와 이 콩들로."

sentences.physical_context: Jack is skeptical about the trade offer.
sentences.korean: "말도 안 돼!" 잭이 말했습니다. "너는 그걸 원하겠지?"

sentences.physical_context: The old man explains the magical nature of the beans.
sentences.korean: "아! 너는 이 콩들이 무엇인지 모르는구나," 노인이 말했습니다. "밤새 심으면 아침에 하늘까지 자라지."

sentences.physical_context: Jack expresses surprise at the old man's claim.
sentences.korean: "정말요?" 잭이 말했습니다. "그럴 리가요."

sentences.physical_context: The old man assures Jack he can have the cow back if the beans don't work.
sentences.korean: "그래, 그렇단다. 만약 그게 사실이 아니면 너는 소를 다시 가져갈 수 있어."

sentences.physical_context: Jack decides to trade the cow for the beans.
sentences.korean: "좋아요," 잭이 말하며 밀키화이트의 고삐를 넘겨주고 콩을 주머니에 넣었습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack returns home before dusk after the trade.
sentences.korean: 잭은 집으로 돌아왔고, 멀리 가지 않았기 때문에 집에 도착했을 때는 아직 어두워지지 않았습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack's mother notices Milky-white is gone and assumes Jack sold her.
sentences.korean: "잭, 돌아왔구나?" 어머니가 말했습니다. "밀키화이트가 없는 걸 보니 팔았구나."

sentences.physical_context: The widow asks Jack how much he got for the cow.
sentences.korean: 얼마에 팔았니?

sentences.physical_context: Jack teases his mother about the trade.
sentences.korean: "어머니는 절대 맞추지 못할 거예요," 잭이 말했습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack's mother is reacting to Jack's return without the cow.
sentences.korean: “아니, 정말이니.

sentences.physical_context: Jack's mother sarcastically praises Jack.
sentences.korean: 잘했구나!

sentences.physical_context: Jack's mother is guessing the amount Jack got for the cow.
sentences.korean: 오 파운드, 십 파운드, 십오 파운드, 아니, 이십 파운드일 리가 없어.

sentences.physical_context: Jack's mother is furious about the trade of the cow for beans.
sentences.korean: “내가 너에게 맞출 수 없다고 말했지, 이 콩들을 어떻게 생각하니; 그들은 마법의 콩이야, 밤새 심어두면----” “뭐라고!” 잭의 어머니가 말했습니다. “너는 정말 바보, 멍청이, 바보가 되어 내 밀키-화이트, 마을에서 가장 좋은 젖소, 그리고 최고의 소고기를 이런 하찮은 콩들로 바꿔버렸구나.

sentences.physical_context: Jack's mother is hitting Jack out of anger.
sentences.korean: 이걸 받아라!

sentences.physical_context: Jack's mother continues to hit Jack.
sentences.korean: 이걸 받아라!

sentences.physical_context: Jack's mother hits Jack again.
sentences.korean: 이걸 받아라!

sentences.physical_context: Jack's mother throws the beans out of the window.
sentences.korean: 그리고 너의 소중한 콩들은 여기 창문 밖으로 나가버려.

sentences.physical_context: Jack's mother sends him to bed without supper.
sentences.korean: 그리고 이제 침대로 가버려.

sentences.physical_context: Jack is forbidden from eating or drinking that night.
sentences.korean: 오늘 밤 너는 한 방울도 마시지 못할 것이고, 한 조각도 삼키지 못할 것이다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack goes to his room in the attic, feeling sad.
sentences.korean: 그래서 잭은 그의 작은 방인 다락방으로 올라갔고, 정말로 슬프고 미안했습니다, 그의 어머니를 위해서나 그의 저녁 식사를 잃은 것에 대해서나.

sentences.physical_context: Jack eventually falls asleep.
sentences.korean: 마침내 그는 잠이 들었습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack wakes up and notices something unusual about the room.
sentences.korean: 그가 깨어났을 때, 방은 매우 이상해 보였습니다.

sentences.physical_context: The sun shines into part of the room, creating a contrast.
sentences.korean: 햇빛이 방의 일부에 비치고 있었고, 나머지는 완전히 어둡고 그늘졌습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack gets up, dresses, and goes to the window.
sentences.korean: 그래서 잭은 일어나 옷을 입고 창문으로 갔습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack sees the beanstalk that has grown from the beans.
sentences.korean: 그리고 무엇을 보았을까요? 그의 어머니가 창문 밖으로 던진 콩들이 자라서 큰 콩나무가 되어 하늘까지 올라가 있었습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack realizes the old man's words were true.
sentences.korean: 결국 그 남자의 말이 사실이었습니다.

sentences.physical_context: The beanstalk is close to Jack's window, allowing him to jump onto it.
sentences.korean: 콩나무는 잭의 창문 바로 옆에 자라 있었기 때문에, 그는 창문을 열고 콩나무로 뛰어오를 수 있었습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack climbs the beanstalk until he reaches the sky.
sentences.korean: 그래서 잭은 올라가고 또 올라가고 또 올라가고 또 올라가고 또 올라가고 또 올라가고 또 올라가서 마침내 하늘에 도달했습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack finds a long road in the sky.
sentences.korean: 그리고 그가 거기에 도착했을 때, 그는 길고 넓은 길이 화살처럼 똑바로 뻗어 있는 것을 발견했습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack walks along the road and finds a big tall house with a big tall woman.
sentences.korean: 그래서 그는 길을 따라 걸어가고 또 걸어가고 또 걸어가다가 큰 키 큰 집에 도착했고, 현관에는 큰 키 큰 여자가 있었습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack politely greets the big tall woman.
sentences.korean: “안녕하세요, 아주머니,” 잭이 아주 공손하게 말했습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack asks the woman for breakfast.
sentences.korean: “아침을 좀 주실 수 있나요?

sentences.physical_context: Jack is very hungry as he hasn't eaten since the previous night.
sentences.korean: 왜냐하면 그는 전날 밤 아무것도 먹지 않았고 사냥꾼처럼 배가 고팠기 때문입니다.

sentences.physical_context: The big tall woman warns Jack to leave or face danger.
sentences.korean: “아침을 원하니, 그렇지?” 큰 키 큰 여자가 말했습니다. “여기서 떠나지 않으면 아침 식사가 될 거야.”

sentences.physical_context: The ogre is described as having a preference for eating boys broiled on toast.
sentences.korean: 내 남자는 오우거인데, 그가 가장 좋아하는 것은 토스트 위에 구운 소년들이다.

sentences.physical_context: The ogre's wife warns Jack to leave before the ogre arrives.
sentences.korean: 어서 떠나지 않으면 그가 곧 올 거야.

sentences.physical_context: Jack pleads with the ogre's wife for something to eat.
sentences.korean: "오! 제발 엄마, 저에게 먹을 것을 주세요, 엄마."

sentences.physical_context: Jack explains he hasn't eaten since yesterday morning.
sentences.korean: "어제 아침부터 아무것도 먹지 못했어요, 정말로요, 엄마," 잭이 말한다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack expresses that he might as well be broiled as die of hunger.
sentences.korean: "굽혀지나 굶어 죽으나 마찬가지예요."

sentences.physical_context: The ogre's wife is shown to be kind-hearted.
sentences.korean: 오우거의 아내는 결국 그렇게 나쁜 사람이 아니었다.

sentences.physical_context: The ogre's wife gives Jack bread, cheese, and milk in the kitchen.
sentences.korean: 그래서 그녀는 잭을 부엌으로 데려가 빵과 치즈, 우유를 주었다.

sentences.physical_context: The house begins to tremble as someone approaches.
sentences.korean: 하지만 잭이 그것들을 다 먹기도 전에 쿵! 쿵! 쿵! 누군가 오는 소리에 집 전체가 떨리기 시작했다.

sentences.physical_context: The ogre's wife exclaims in surprise.
sentences.korean: "어머나 세상에!

sentences.physical_context: The ogre's wife realizes the ogre is coming and is worried.
sentences.korean: 내 남편이야," 오우거의 아내가 말했다, "어떻게 해야 하지?

sentences.physical_context: The ogre's wife tells Jack to hide quickly.
sentences.korean: 여기, 빨리 와서 여기로 뛰어들어.

sentences.physical_context: The ogre's wife hides Jack in the oven as the ogre enters.
sentences.korean: 그리고 그녀는 오우거가 들어오자마자 잭을 오븐에 밀어넣었다.

sentences.physical_context: The ogre is described as being very large.
sentences.korean: 그는 정말로 큰 사람이었다.

sentences.physical_context: The ogre unhooks calves from his belt and commands his wife to broil them.
sentences.korean: 그는 허리띠에 매달린 송아지 세 마리를 풀어 테이블에 던지며 말했다: "여보, 아침으로 이 중 두 마리를 구워줘."

sentences.physical_context: The ogre smells something unusual.
sentences.korean: 아, 이게 무슨 냄새지?

sentences.physical_context: The ogre recites a threatening rhyme about smelling an Englishman.
sentences.korean: 피-파이-포-펌, 나는 영국인의 피 냄새를 맡는다, 살아있든 죽어있든 그의 뼈로 내 빵을 갈아먹을 것이다.

sentences.physical_context: The ogre's wife tries to reassure the ogre that he's imagining things.
sentences.korean: "말도 안 돼요, 여보," 그의 아내가 말했다, "당신은 꿈을 꾸고 있어요.

sentences.physical_context: The ogre's wife suggests the smell is from yesterday's meal.
sentences.korean: 아니면 어제 저녁에 당신이 좋아했던 그 작은 소년의 냄새일지도 몰라요.

sentences.physical_context: The ogre's wife suggests the ogre wash up while she prepares breakfast.
sentences.korean: 여기, 가서 씻고 정리하세요, 그러면 당신이 돌아올 때쯤이면 아침이 준비될 거예요.

sentences.physical_context: The ogre leaves, and Jack is about to escape but is stopped by the woman.
sentences.korean: 그래서 오우거는 떠났고, 잭은 오븐에서 뛰쳐나가 도망치려 했지만 여자가 그를 막았다.

sentences.physical_context: The woman advises Jack to wait until the ogre is asleep.
sentences.korean: "그가 잠들 때까지 기다리세요," 그녀가 말했다; "그는 항상 아침 식사 후에 낮잠을 자요.

sentences.physical_context: The ogre counts gold until he falls asleep, shaking the house with his snores.
sentences.korean: 오우거는 아침 식사를 하고 나서 큰 상자에서 금주머니 두 개를 꺼내 앉아 세다가 결국 그의 머리가 끄덕여지기 시작하고 코를 골기 시작하여 집 전체가 다시 흔들렸다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack sneaks out, steals a bag of gold, and escapes down the beanstalk.
sentences.korean: 그러자 잭은 살금살금 오븐에서 나와 오우거를 지나가면서 금주머니 하나를 팔에 끼고, 콩나무로 달려가서 금주머니를 던졌고, 그것은 물론 그의 어머니의 정원에 떨어졌고, 그는 내려가고 내려가서 결국 집에 도착하여 그의 어머니에게 금을 보여주며 말했다: "어머니, 콩이 정말로 마법적이지 않았나요."

sentences.physical_context: Jack shows his mother the gold and claims the beans are magical.
sentences.korean: 그들은 정말로 마법적이에요, 보세요.

sentences.physical_context: Jack decides to try his luck again with the beanstalk after the gold runs out.
sentences.korean: 그래서 그들은 금주머니로 한동안 살았지만 결국 그것이 다 떨어지자 잭은 콩나무 꼭대기로 다시 운을 시험해보기로 결심했다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack climbs the beanstalk and reaches the road near the big tall house.
sentences.korean: 그래서 어느 맑은 아침에 그는 일찍 일어나 콩나무에 올라타고 계속해서 올라가서 마침내 다시 길에 도착했고 전에 갔던 큰 키 큰 집에 도착했습니다.

sentences.physical_context: The big tall woman stands on the doorstep of the house.
sentences.korean: 거기, 정말로, 문간에 서 있는 큰 키 큰 여자가 있었습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack greets the woman and asks for food.
sentences.korean: "좋은 아침입니다, 아주머니," 잭이 대담하게 말했습니다. "무엇 좀 먹을 것을 주실 수 있나요?"

sentences.physical_context: The woman warns Jack that her husband might eat him.
sentences.korean: "가버려, 얘야," 큰 키 큰 여자가 말했습니다. "안 그러면 내 남편이 너를 아침으로 먹어버릴 거야."

sentences.physical_context: The woman recognizes Jack from a previous visit.
sentences.korean: 하지만 너는 전에 여기 왔던 그 젊은이가 아니니?

sentences.physical_context: The woman mentions her husband missed a bag of gold.
sentences.korean: 알고 있니, 그날 내 남편이 금 가방 하나를 잃어버렸어.

sentences.physical_context: Jack claims he can't speak due to hunger.
sentences.korean: "그거 참 이상하네요, 아주머니," 잭이 말했습니다. "제가 그 일에 대해 뭔가 말할 수 있을 것 같은데 너무 배고파서 먹을 것을 먹기 전까지는 말을 할 수가 없어요."

sentences.physical_context: The woman, curious, gives Jack something to eat.
sentences.korean: 큰 키 큰 여자는 너무 궁금해서 그를 데리고 들어가 먹을 것을 주었습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack hides in the oven as the giant's footsteps are heard.
sentences.korean: 하지만 그가 천천히 먹기 시작했을 때 쿵! 쿵! 쿵! 그들은 거인의 발소리를 들었고 그의 아내는 잭을 오븐에 숨겼습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Events unfold as they did previously.
sentences.korean: 모든 것이 이전과 같이 일어났습니다.

sentences.physical_context: The ogre enters and has breakfast.
sentences.korean: 오거가 들어와서 이전처럼 말했습니다: "피-파-포-펌," 그리고 세 마리의 구운 황소로 아침을 먹었습니다.

sentences.physical_context: The ogre asks for the hen that lays golden eggs.
sentences.korean: 그러고 나서 그는 말했습니다: "아내, 황금 알을 낳는 암탉을 가져와."

sentences.physical_context: The hen lays a golden egg on command.
sentences.korean: 그래서 그녀가 그것을 가져왔고, 오거는 말했습니다: "낳아라," 그러자 그것은 황금 알을 낳았습니다.

sentences.physical_context: The ogre begins to nod off and snore.
sentences.korean: 그리고 나서 오거는 고개를 끄덕이며 코를 골기 시작했고 집이 흔들렸습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack sneaks out and steals the golden hen.
sentences.korean: 그러자 잭은 오븐에서 살금살금 나와 황금 암탉을 잡고 "잭 로빈슨"이라고 말하기도 전에 도망쳤습니다.

sentences.physical_context: The hen cackles, waking the ogre as Jack escapes.
sentences.korean: 하지만 이번에는 암탉이 꼬꼬댁거려 오거를 깨웠고, 잭이 집을 나서자마자 그는 "아내, 아내, 내 황금 암탉을 어떻게 했어?"라고 외치는 소리를 들었습니다.

sentences.physical_context: The wife responds to the ogre's call.
sentences.korean: 그리고 아내가 말했습니다: "왜요, 여보?"

sentences.physical_context: Jack rushes to the beanstalk and climbs down quickly.
sentences.korean: 하지만 잭이 들은 것은 그것뿐이었고, 그는 콩나무로 달려가 불붙은 집처럼 내려갔습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack shows his mother the hen and it lays a golden egg.
sentences.korean: 그리고 집에 도착했을 때 그는 어머니에게 멋진 암탉을 보여주고 "낳아라"라고 말했습니다. 그러자 그것은 매번 "낳아라"라고 말할 때마다 황금 알을 낳았습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack decides to try his luck again at the beanstalk.
sentences.korean: 하지만 잭은 만족하지 않았고, 얼마 지나지 않아 다시 콩나무 꼭대기에서 운을 시험해 보기로 결심했습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack climbs the beanstalk again to the top.
sentences.korean: 그래서 어느 맑은 아침에 그는 일찍 일어나 콩나무로 가서 계속해서 올라가서 꼭대기에 도착했습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack decides not to go directly to the ogre's house.
sentences.korean: 하지만 이번에는 오거의 집으로 바로 가지 않기로 했습니다.

sentences.physical_context: Jack waits and sneaks into the house when the ogre's wife leaves.
sentences.korean: 그리고 그가 집 근처에 도착했을 때 그는 오거의 아내가 물을 뜨러 나오는 것을 보고 기다렸다가 집으로 몰래 들어가 구리통에 숨었습니다.
